source: JZ Mock A · Paper 2 · Question 11 · Publisher worked answer
label: JZ Mock A · Paper 2 · Question 11
knowledgePattern: Compare signed trigonometric areas to prove both implication directions
solution:
Write C(t)=∫0tcosxdx and G(t)=∫0tcos3(2x)dx. We use areas and graph symmetry, rather than trigonometric antiderivatives.

The graph of cos3(2x) has period π. Its equal positive and negative quarter-period lobes cancel, so G(π/2)=G(π)=0, and each complete period contributes zero. Similarly C(π)=0. Hence every integer multiple of π makes the requested integral zero.

For 0<t≤π/4, the integrands obey 0≤cos3(2x)<cosx at interior positive inputs up to t. Thus 0<G(t)<C(t). For π/4≤t≤π/2, G decreases to zero while C increases, so 0≤G(t)<C(t) still holds.

For π/2<t<π, put u=π−t. Reflection of the two graphs gives C(t)=C(u)>0 and G(t)=−G(u). Therefore |G(t)|<C(t) throughout 0<t<π.

For a nonnegative endpoint k=nπ+t with integer n≥0 and 0≤t<π, the complete blocks cancel. The remaining cosine area is (−1)nC(t) and the remaining cubed-cosine area is G(t). If t>0, their sum cannot vanish because |G(t)|<C(t). It is zero when t=0.

The full integrand is even, so reversing a positive endpoint to its negative reverses the integral. The same zero set therefore holds for negative k. Precisely the integer multiples of π work, including zero. P is necessary and sufficient for Q. Answer A.

hints.title: Separate the two accumulated areas
hints.body: Sketch the two integrands over a full period. Identify their sign changes and the symmetries of equal positive and negative lobes.
hints.recap: The whole trigonometric input determines the period; cosine is even.
hints.pitfall: A zero total over one block does not prove that no smaller partial area vanishes.
hints.pause: Work out the contribution of complete blocks before considering partial ones.

recall.reminder: The whole trigonometric input determines the period; cosine is even.

hints.title: Compare the sizes on a short interval
hints.body: On 0<x<π/4, compare cos3(2x) with cosx using the range and ordering of cosine.
hints.recap: A strict pointwise ordering on the interior of a forward interval gives a strict ordering of the integrals.
hints.pitfall: Keep the interval restriction when using monotonicity of cosine.
hints.pause: Establish an area comparison without calculating either antiderivative.

recall.reminder: A strict pointwise ordering on the interior of a forward interval gives a strict ordering of the integrals.

hints.title: Extend the comparison by symmetry
hints.body: After the quarter-period, track which accumulated area increases or decreases. Relate an endpoint t in the second half of [0,π] to π−t.
hints.recap: Equal reflected lobes have equal geometric areas, but opposite signs may make their integrals cancel.
hints.pitfall: Compare signed areas, not just the individual function heights at the endpoint.
hints.pause: Decide whether the partial areas can cancel each other before the end of the block.

recall.reminder: Equal reflected lobes have equal geometric areas, but opposite signs may make their integrals cancel.

hints.title: Finish both directions
hints.body: Reduce a general endpoint to complete blocks and one remainder. Check zero and negative endpoints as well before classifying the condition.
hints.recap: Sufficiency and necessity are separate directions; each needs justification.
hints.pitfall: Showing that the stated endpoints work proves only one direction.
hints.pause: Determine the complete zero set of the accumulated sum and compare it with P.

recall.reminder: Sufficiency and necessity are separate directions; each needs justification.
